implementation_notes: Swift 5.7's Clock/Instant model turns an expiry into a value: ContinuousClock.now + .seconds(30) is a monotonic deadline, Task.sleep(until:deadline, clock:.continuous) suspends until it (optionally with tolerance), and cancelling the surrounding task aborts the wait - so an in-process work item is simply a task raced against its deadline. ContinuousClock keeps advancing while the device sleeps, which is what message freshness means, whereas Date is a settable wall clock only suitable for the absolute timestamps on the wire. Swift has no first-party broker client, so crossing a process means speaking the transport's TTL contract (AMQP expiration, JMS time-to-live) directly and converting the header into a local Instant at each hop.
pitfalls: Task.sleep throws CancellationError when its task is cancelled (including the group cancellation above); catching that generically and continuing turns cancellation into silent stale processing.
ContinuousClock.Instant is process-local and cannot be sent over the wire; Date-based deadlines are settable, so pick per side: absolute Date for the wire, ContinuousClock for local waits.
Structured concurrency cancels the group but not code that ignores cancellation: a handler stuck in a synchronous loop still has to check Task.isCancelled (or its own deadline) explicitly.
